prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening a new regime of precision tests of nature

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: one part, B022, Katori and Ye. After the full exchange I still hold it for a reason of mechanism and not of count. Magic-wavelength trapping is a simple and general statement: tune the lattice so that the differential light shift of the two clock levels vanishes, and the trap confines atoms without perturbing the transition, so that many atoms are read out at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. That is why the stability and the systematic control reach 10^-18, and why the result is understood and not merely working: blackbody shifts, polarizabilities and collisional shifts are all computed and checked, and independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) agree at that level. The consequences are physical. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a sample, limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter, and the Fermi-degenerate many-body clock regime show that the instrument probes physics and does not only count it. On the chair's wording question, I would accept either 'invention' or 'development' alone but prefer to carry both, because Katori's concept and Ye's record regime are different contributions and the two-name credit follows exactly that division. I would keep the forward-looking phrase short and factual, because the citation should state what has been done and not promise dark matter.
statement.case_against: The honest objection remains distinctness and the discovery-versus-tool question. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize already honoured the metrology lineage, and the largest scientific returns from lattice clocks so far are upper limits and consistency tests with no new effect seen. The redefinition of the second has not happened. Credit also extends beyond two names (Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, the comb pioneers), and I cannot verify independent priority for the magic-wavelength proposal from the packet. I weigh these as real but not decisive: the first is answered by the citation naming the lattice architecture and not metrology in general, the second by what is already demonstrated, and the third by the three-person limit together with the clear division of contribution between Katori and Ye. If the committee wanted a second part, no candidate I can support fits within the limit of three unique people alongside the two names.

responses.point: Kroll states that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes because it concerns a different route to precision, many neutral atoms in a lattice, and admits that the discovery-versus-measurement question is the one on which colleagues may disagree with him. He also discloses a mild personal link to the community through John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with the distinctness argument and would use it as the core of the answer to the chair's question: the earlier prizes concern producing and counting frequency and controlling a single ion, whereas the lattice clock is a statistical advantage, with the number of atoms, engineered by a cancellation condition. That is a mechanism, and it can be written in one clause of the citation. On your disclosure, I think disclosure is sufficient. You report no direct tie to Katori or Ye, and a year in a laboratory that is connected to a collaborator of Ye's is the kind of field closeness that every member here has with some candidate. I would not ask for a step beyond that, and I would not remove your voice from a B022 discussion on this basis.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, observes that the discovery content of B022 so far is mostly upper limits and consistency tests with no new effect observed, and notes that Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team.
responses.response: The upper-limit point is correct and I would not hide it. But the demonstrated content is not only limits: the gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres and the quantum-degenerate many-body clock are positive, quantitative observations that the instrument made possible and that no earlier clock could make. That is what the citation should lean on if it needs to answer the discovery question. On Ye's share, a Nobel credit to a laboratory leader for work done with a large team is the usual pattern and is not special to this entry; the question for the committee is whether the named person defined the programme, and for the record regime the evidence points to Ye. I would rather see this stated in the citation as 'development' than split the credit across JILA co-authors, since that would break the three-person limit without improving accuracy.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second as an external endorsement, and says that if B022 were judged only a tool, B020 is the more conceptually rich alternative.
responses.response: I would not wait. The scientific content, the 10^-18 performance and its reproduction in several laboratories, is already in place, and the redefinition is a metrological and diplomatic procedure that follows from it. Making the prize depend on that procedure would turn the committee into a follower of the standards bodies. On B020 I take your point that it is conceptually rich, and I rank it as my first alternative now, ahead of B011, because it is the only fallback with broad support. But the credited-name problem is real: five names for three places, with the contributions of Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger and Cirac distributed in ways I cannot sort from the packet. That is why it is a fallback and not a second part.

responses.point: Eriksson says that B022 is an instrument and measurement achievement and not the discovery of a new state of matter, and that the committee has recently honoured frequency combs and ion-based metrology, so some will say this is the same territory again. Eriksson also values the independent reproduction across laboratories.
responses.response: I accept that it is not a new state of matter, and the citation should not suggest otherwise. My view is that the Nobel tradition in physics has always included advances in what can be measured, provided the underlying mechanism is identified and the result is robust, and your own criterion of independent reproduction is met here more strongly than for most entries on the list. I would add from the statistical-physics side that the lattice clock's advantage is not only engineering: the stability follows from the number of interrogated atoms and the cancellation of the light shift, which is a clean piece of physics. I also note, as you do for B018, that I would not let a method or tool without a clear mechanism carry the prize, and I do not think B022 is that.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge yes, but this is a judgement about prize-level novelty.

Priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal against other early lattice-clock proposals and demonstrations has not been verified from the provided files, and the credit of Lemonde and others rests on this.

Whether a second part could be justified: B020 would need a defensible set of names that fits within the three-person limit alongside Katori and Ye, which I do not see, so I cannot propose a two-part prize.
Whether the citation can carry the 'new regime of precision tests' phrase without overstating results that are so far upper limits and consistency checks.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict applies to B022. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am in the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson, which has no bearing on this candidate. I have no stated connection to B020, B011 or B048 beyond general research interest. I note Kroll's disclosure and consider disclosure sufficient.
